title: Most US Data Center Power Demand Will Never Materialize, Analysts Warn
excerpt: BloombergNEF nearly doubled its forecast for data center electricity consumption, but developers are filing far more power requests than projects they intend to build — and household bills are climbing as a result.
body:
• BloombergNEF projects US data center power demand could reach 194 gigawatts by 2035, an 83% increase from its December forecast, accounting for roughly 20% of national electricity consumption.
  • Many planned data centers will never be built — developers file 5 to 10 times more power requests than projects that actually materialize, leaving utilities and ratepayers exposed to costly stranded infrastructure.
  • New York enacted the first statewide moratorium on data center development, and 15 state legislatures have considered temporary bans as residential electricity bills have climbed 29.3% since 2020.
  • Hyperscalers including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta could collectively spend $700 billion on data center infrastructure this year, even as political opposition intensifies.

The gap between what AI data centers say they need and what the US power grid can deliver is widening fast — and the consequences are already hitting household electricity bills.

BloombergNEF projects that US data center power capacity could reach 194 gigawatts by 2035, an 83% jump from its December forecast. At that level, data centers would consume roughly 20% of the nation's electricity, up from 5.9% today. But industry analysts and utility executives increasingly agree that much of that demand will never materialize.

A Pipeline Full of Phantom Projects

The core problem is straightforward: developers are filing far more power requests than they intend to fulfill. According to Astrid Atkinson, a former Google senior director of software engineering, utilities are seeing five to 10 times more interconnection requests than data centers actually being built. Developers simultaneously file power demands with multiple utilities while negotiating tax incentives across states, leaving utilities exposed when projects relocate or cancel.

https://x.com/Newsforce/status/2086920225581306337

"Every coal plant, every gas plant, every solar farm in the US — one unit of energy out of five generated by them is going to data centers."

— Lloyd Arnold, Analyst, BloombergNEF

Mark Daly, BNEF's head of technology and innovation, acknowledged that the US is "a really tough environment to build data centers right now." Competition for labor and power equipment is fiercer than ever, grid interconnection delays persist, and the majority of new projects are sponsored by first-time developers with limited execution experience.

Rising Bills and Growing Backlash

The financial burden is increasingly falling on residential customers. A ConsumerAffairs analysis found that the average US residential electric bill has risen 29.3% since 2020, driven partly by infrastructure investment to serve large data center loads. In some states, the spike has been far steeper — Connecticut saw an 18.4% increase in a single year, and Maine reported a 36.3% jump.

Bill Gates added his voice to the debate in June, warning Big Tech on CNBC that ordinary electricity customers should not be left subsidizing AI infrastructure costs. The Microsoft co-founder pointed to a growing list of stalled projects: 48 data center developments worth $156 billion were blocked or delayed in 2025, with another 20 failing in Q1 2026 alone.

The political response is accelerating. Fifteen state legislatures have considered temporary bans on data center development, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. New York Governor Kathy Hochul enacted the first statewide moratorium, giving regulators up to a year to craft rules protecting ratepayers, the environment, and the grid. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in June found that 57% of Americans oppose building data centers in their communities.

Hyperscalers Press Ahead Regardless

Despite the headwinds, the biggest players show no signs of slowing down. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta could collectively spend $700 billion on data center infrastructure this year, according to their quarterly earnings calls. Nearly 200 entities signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge with President Trump, promising that AI data centers' power consumption won't drive up consumer bills.

"If the projected data centre load doesn't fully materialise — which all evidence and, frankly, common sense at this point is pointing to — ratepayers will ultimately bear that economic burden."

— Megan Gibson, Southern Environmental Law Center

BNEF tracked 124 gigawatts of announced on-site gas capacity as developers try to circumvent lengthy grid interconnection queues, though only a small fraction is under construction. The lone off-grid facility completed so far — SpaceX's Colossus 2 project in Memphis — relied on dozens of unpermitted, highly polluting gas generators to come online in record time.

What's Next

The disconnect between announced capacity and actual builds raises fundamental questions about who bears the risk. Utilities that invest billions in new generation and transmission infrastructure based on inflated demand forecasts may end up with stranded assets — costs that would inevitably flow through to household ratepayers. As the AI boom reshapes America's energy landscape, the battle over who pays for it is only getting louder.
